author: A Robot
objectives: Students will describe the apparent path of Mars across the night sky during a retrograde episode, including the eastward drift, westward loop, and return to eastward motion.
Students will explain why apparent retrograde motion occurs in the heliocentric model as a consequence of Earth overtaking a slower-moving outer planet.
Students will contrast the geocentric and heliocentric explanations of retrograde motion and articulate why the heliocentric model is preferred on grounds of parsimony.
Students will predict when retrograde motion will occur for a given outer planet based on the relative orbital positions of Earth and that planet.
Students will compare the apparent retrograde loops of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, and explain why more distant planets produce smaller loops.

modules.description: Observation of Mars's apparent retrograde loop in the night sky.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Describe the apparent path of Mars across the night sky during a retrograde episode.

clips.changeMeaning: Sets up the night sky and identifies Mars against the constellations.
clips.narration: Welcome to the night sky. Look at the constellations of the ecliptic around you. That distinct red point of light is the planet Mars.

clips.changeMeaning: Animates Mars drifting slowly eastward.
clips.narration: Over the course of weeks, if you plotted Mars's position night after night, you would see it drift slowly eastward against the background stars.

clips.changeMeaning: Animates the westward loop (retrograde motion) of Mars.
clips.narration: But roughly every 26 months, something strange happens. Mars slows down, halts, and begins moving backward—westward—for about two months, tracing a loop in the sky. This is apparent retrograde motion.

clips.changeMeaning: Animates Mars resuming its normal eastward path.
clips.narration: Finally, it slows again, halts, and resumes its normal eastward motion. This bizarre behavior was the central puzzle of pre-modern astronomy. Why would a planet move backward?

modules.description: Exploration of the geocentric explanation using epicycles and deferents.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Contrast the geocentric and heliocentric explanations of retrograde motion.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduces the geocentric model components.
clips.narration: Ancient astronomers proposed the geocentric model to explain this. Here, Earth sits at the center of the universe.

clips.changeMeaning: Starts the epicycle machinery to demonstrate retrograde motion.
clips.narration: To create the backward loop, Mars rides on a small circle called an epicycle, which itself rides on a larger circle called a deferent. As Mars reaches the inside of its epicycle closest to Earth, it appears to move backward.

clips.changeMeaning: Adds text highlighting the complexity of the model.
clips.narration: While this model reproduced the loop, it required carefully tuned speeds and circle sizes. As data improved, astronomers had to stack epicycles upon epicycles just to keep predictions accurate.

modules.description: The heliocentric model demonstrating Earth overtaking Mars.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain why apparent retrograde motion occurs in the heliocentric model as a consequence of Earth overtaking a slower-moving outer planet.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduces the heliocentric (Sun-centered) model.
clips.narration: Now let's switch to the heliocentric view. The Sun sits at the center. Earth orbits at 1 Astronomical Unit, and Mars orbits further out at 1.52 AU.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the relative speeds of Earth and Mars.
clips.narration: Notice that Earth, being closer to the Sun, moves faster. Roughly every 26 months, Earth catches up to and overtakes Mars on the inside track.

clips.changeMeaning: Explains that the loop is naturally produced without epicycles.
clips.narration: Watch as Earth swings past Mars. From Earth's perspective, this overtaking creates the illusion that Mars is moving backward. No epicycles are needed—just two smooth ellipses.

modules.description: Simultaneous view of heliocentric orbits and the resulting night-sky line of sight.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Link the physical mechanism of overtaking to the visual phenomenon of the retrograde loop.

components.scriptDescription: Draws a line starting from Earth's transform, passing through Mars's transform, and extending outward to a distant sphere to indicate the line of sight against the stars.

clips.changeMeaning: Activates a line of sight component to connect Earth and Mars positions to the background stars.
clips.narration: Let's link the two views. The line stretching from Earth through Mars points to Mars's apparent position against the stars. Normally, this line sweeps eastward.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the moment Earth overtakes Mars, causing the line to sweep westward.
clips.narration: But as Earth begins to overtake Mars, look at the line! It reverses direction and sweeps westward. At that exact moment, an observer on Earth sees Mars trace its backward loop.

clips.changeMeaning: Resumes normal eastward motion after passing.
clips.narration: Once Earth has passed Mars, the line resumes its eastward sweep. The retrograde loop is a real apparent motion produced purely by orbital geometry.

modules.description: An embodied activity where the user walks Earth's orbit to see the parallax effect.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Experience the relative motion effect firsthand to solidify understanding of apparent motion.
instructions: Look at the red Mars sphere.
Walk slowly along the highlighted ring on the floor around the center of the room.

clips.changeMeaning: Instructs the user to walk along Earth's orbit.
clips.narration: Now it's your turn. You are standing on Earth's orbit. The red sphere in front of you is Mars. Slowly walk sideways along the circular path on the floor, keeping your eyes on Mars.

clips.changeMeaning: Guides the user through the point of closest approach.
clips.narration: As you pass the point closest to Mars, notice how Mars appears to drift backward against the distant background stars. You are physically recreating the retrograde effect simply by passing a slower object!

modules.description: Comparing the retrograde loops of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Compare the apparent retrograde loops of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, and explain why more distant planets produce smaller loops.

clips.changeMeaning: Shows Mars's orbit and its retrograde loop size.
clips.narration: Let's compare the outer planets. We've seen that Mars produces a retrograde loop about 15 degrees across.

clips.changeMeaning: Shows Jupiter and Saturn orbits and their respective loop sizes.
clips.narration: Now look at Jupiter at 5.2 AU and Saturn at 9.5 AU. Their retrograde loops are much smaller—Jupiter's is about 10 degrees, and Saturn's is just 7 degrees.

clips.changeMeaning: Explains the relationship between distance and loop size.
clips.narration: Why? Because they are farther away. Earth's orbital motion subtends a smaller angle when viewed from a greater distance. It's the same reason nearby objects shift more than distant ones when you move your head.

modules.description: An interactive challenge to predict where retrograde motion occurs.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Predict when retrograde motion will occur for a given outer planet based on relative orbital positions.

components.scriptDescription: Checks if Mars is dragged to be aligned with Earth (Sun-Earth-Mars angle near zero). Fires success event triggering clip_2_prediction_success when true.

components.text: Drag Mars to the Opposition position

clips.changeMeaning: Explains the task to drag Mars to the correct location for a retrograde event.
clips.narration: Challenge time! Earth is currently paused in its orbit. Grab Mars and drag it to the position on its orbit where an observer on Earth would currently see retrograde motion.

clips.changeMeaning: Waits for the user to complete the puzzle.
clips.narration: Excellent! Retrograde motion occurs near opposition, when Earth and Mars are aligned on the same side of the Sun, poised for Earth to overtake.

modules.description: A recap of the five main concepts covered in the lab.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Synthesize the observational, geocentric, and heliocentric perspectives on retrograde motion.

clips.changeMeaning: Displays the recap of the phenomenon and geocentric model.
clips.narration: To review: We first observed Mars trace a retrograde loop in the night sky. We then saw how ancient astronomers used complex epicycles to explain it.

components.text: 3. Heliocentric Resolution\n4. Linked Perspectives\n5. Parallax of Outer Planets

clips.changeMeaning: Updates the recap text to highlight the heliocentric model.
clips.narration: Next, the heliocentric model resolved the puzzle simply: Earth, moving faster on the inside track, overtakes Mars. We linked this orbital overtaking directly to the backward loop seen in the sky, and discovered that more distant outer planets show smaller loops.
